html.sum.jump: ↓ Everything below is the evidence and mechanism detail, and every item can be opened up and checked
html.what.title: What this is
html.what.p1: IdentityMD ($IMD) is a token on Ethereum. The protocol opened its own Uniswap v4 pool and attached an automatic program (a hook) to it. What that program does is this: once the IMD sitting in the pool passes a certain amount, the excess is pulled out and destroyed — 85% of it burned permanently and 15% distributed to stakers.
html.what.p2: That mechanism keeps IMD deflationary, and it is where staking yield comes from. So whether it is still running matters directly to holders and stakers.
html.what.p3: This page answers two questions: is the burning still working? And if it has stopped, how much more IMD is needed before it restarts?
html.what.quoteLabel: Design intent · from the team's on-chain messages
html.what.quote1Note: In other words: when people are selling, the hook buys IMD cheap, burns 85% of it and hands the rest to long-term holders. The result is that stakers earn rewards while long-term holders' share of the network grows over time — a double incentive.
html.what.quote2Note: It does not exist for IMD alone: several live tokens (some with a higher market cap) have asked to use this hook, and the team is turning it into a component other tokens can reuse. That also explains why the launcher (CappedBurnLauncher) is permissionless — anyone can use it to open a burn pool of their own.
html.what.readonly: Every number is read straight from Ethereum and Base (read-only calls: no wallet, no signing, no transactions) and refreshed every 60 seconds. The i next to a figure opens up the contract and the function it came from. Anything that cannot be read says “unavailable” and explains why, instead of showing a 0.

html.doors.title: Burning has two doors
html.doors.lede1: What this means: even if the first door recovers, destruction will not happen on its own — the second door needs someone to pay gas and call it on Base.
html.doors.lede2: The first door is on Ethereum: once the IMD in the pool passes the line it is pulled out and handed to a waypoint contract. The second door is on Base: someone bridges the IMD out of that waypoint contract and calls burn. Both of the two doors need someone to push them — a person or a bot.

html.sim.title: When it will start burning again
html.sim.lede: What this means: the IMD stacked up in the pool has to climb back above the trigger line. Below you can adjust how much IMD is sold into the pool each day and see how long the gap takes to close. You can also leave every input alone and just read the default result.

html.sim.inflowHint: When someone sells IMD the pool's inventory grows, moving it closer to the trigger line
html.sim.priceLabel: Assume IMD's price moves against ETH
html.sim.priceHint: When IMD loses value the pool ends up holding more IMD, making a trigger likelier

html.sim.techSummary: Details for technical readers: the maths behind the simulator and its known simplifications
html.sim.techBody:
held = L × (sqrtP − sqrtP_lower) / 2^96 (L339-341, rounded down); the trigger line decays as newCap = max(cap − (cap−held)·ratchetBps/10000, cap − capDecay·elapsed/86400, capFloor) (L963-969); the amount pulled out is floor(L × excess / held) (L997), split into rewarded = floor(removed × rewardShareBps / 10000) (L1033-1034).
Known simplifications: the model does not reproduce AMM slippage or fees; it does not predict price (price is an input); and “net inflow” is an outcome of trading in a real pool, not something that can be set independently.
The model has been reproduced end-to-end against real historical trim events: the liquidity it computes matches the on-chain event wei for wei.
html.trimnow.title: How much would burn if it triggered right now
html.trimnow.note: A note on rounding: every pull-out rounds down on its own, so adding up rewards / total across all historical trims gives 1499 bps rather than the configured 1500 bps. A single split is exactly 1500 bps. The owner has not changed the rate.
html.rewards.title: Why staking rewards are zero
html.rewards.lede: What this means: with burning stopped, the 15% that goes to stakers has stopped with it. The money in the two buckets below sits there by design rather than by accident — but it can be taken out by the owner.
html.rewards.techSummary: Details for technical readers: the three buckets and why the funds stay put
html.rewards.techBody:
RewardDistributor splits rewards into three buckets by stakingBps / bondingBps / nftBps. The source comment reads “Only the staking bucket is routed today”; the bonding and NFT buckets are bookkeeping only, to be moved later with emergencyWithdraw() (L92-99). There is no such switch as BONDING_LIVE in the source.
The owner of RewardDripper can call rescueERC20() (L178-181) to withdraw the entire reward buffer.

watch.src.renounceOwnership: Ownable — renounceOwnership() sets the owner to 0x0
owner.what.closeMarket: Withdraws the entire market position (all IMD + ETH), and marketOpen can never return to true (the L580 comment reads: Terminal).
owner.what.withdrawFees: Withdraws all accumulated LP fees (both the token side and the ETH side).
owner.what.withdrawRetainedEth: Withdraws the retainedEth that was set aside for the backstop.
owner.what.dripperRescue: Sweeps the whole reward buffer (IMD) — the staking rewards that are sitting there waiting to be released.
owner.what.simdRescue: Sweeps any ERC20 balance — including every staker's IMD (totalAssets).
owner.what.simdPause: Freezes every deposit, mint, withdrawal and redemption (renouncing is blocked while paused, L165-168).
owner.what.distributorWithdraw: Withdraws this contract's entire IMD balance, including the heldBonding + heldNft buckets sitting idle here.
owner.what.burnExecutorRescue: Withdraws the IMD waiting to be bridged to Base (the current queue size is in the “second door” card above).
owner.what.imdSetPeer: Changes the bridge peer: the receiving contract on Base can be pointed at any address, which changes where bridged tokens are burned.
owner.what.imdSetDelegate: Changes the LayerZero delegate, which can in turn alter the messaging library and the security configuration.
owner.note.simd.renounced: Ownership renounced: owner = 0x0, so rescueERC20 and setPaused no longer work. No admin can move or freeze stakers' IMD any more.
owner.note.simd.live: The owner is still an EOA — staked funds can be withdrawn, and every deposit and withdrawal can be frozen with one call.
owner.note.hook.live: The owner is still an EOA — the entire market position (all IMD + ETH) can be withdrawn at any moment, and that cannot be undone.
owner.note.dripper.live: The owner is still an EOA — the whole reward buffer can be swept.
owner.note.distributor.live: The owner is still an EOA — this contract's entire IMD balance can be withdrawn, idle buckets included.
owner.note.burnExecutor.live: The owner is still an EOA — the IMD waiting to be bridged can be withdrawn, and the bridge destination can be changed.
owner.note.imd.live: The owner is still an EOA — the bridge peer configuration can be changed, which moves where bridged tokens land.

So that time only means "no later than", and more burns may have happened since. Live on-chain numbers (block, ignition distance, balances) are unaffected.

html.howto.summary: Tutorial: how to post an on-chain message
html.howto.intro: Beyond Twitter and the docs site, the team also reads the on-chain messages sent to this address — anyone can post, no permission needed and no IMD required. Here is the whole procedure.
html.howto.step1: Write what you want to say first. Plain UTF-8 text only — it is recorded on Ethereum permanently and publicly. Never include anything private: a key, a seed phrase, an email address, your real name. Once it is on-chain it cannot be taken back.
html.howto.step2: Start an ordinary transfer in your wallet.Recipient 0x200E710aCAA6A93bbc77146026328C40F1d60fB1Set the amount to 0 ETH — this address is the dev's plain wallet, so ETH sent here is a gift, not a requirement. The network must be Ethereum mainnet (chainId 1).
html.howto.step3: Put the text into the "Hex data" field. Most wallets hide it under advanced options (MetaMask calls it Hex data, Rabby calls it Data). What goes in is the text encoded as hex — the converter below does that for you, in your browser only. Nothing is uploaded.
html.howto.step4: Confirm and send; you pay the gas. Roughly a few dollars on Ethereum mainnet. About a minute later the message shows up in the list above — this page re-reads the chain every 60 seconds.
html.howto.warn: Three things to settle before you send: messages are public and permanent — anyone can read them and nobody can delete them; your sender address is recorded alongside it, so use an address you are happy to have public; this page only reads these messages — it never posts for you, never holds funds, never charges a fee. Do not hand a private key to anyone who claims they will post it for you.
